idiom_name: class exposing List<T> via an explicit backing field / backing property
implementation_notes: Kotlin's read-only/mutable collection split does the boundary work: keep the data in a `private val _lines = mutableListOf<OrderLine>()` and expose `val lines: List<OrderLine>`, or - on current compilers - declare `val lines: List<OrderLine> field = mutableListOf()`, where 'the compiler uses the public property type List outside the class, so API users can only read what's in the list'. The explicit-backing-field syntax is a recent addition, so the backing-property form remains the portable fallback. Mutating functions re-establish the invariant, value parts are data classes/value classes, other aggregates are referenced by id, and persistence is the JVM stack (JPA/Hibernate or Spring Data as in Java) since no Kotlin-specific aggregate library exists.
pitfalls: `List` is a read-only view, not an immutable copy: a caller can cast it back to MutableList, so use `lines.toList()` when the collection crosses a module boundary or is handed to untrusted code.
`val` only freezes the reference: returning the backing MutableList from an internal helper and storing it in a public property makes the mutable collection public.
Data-class `copy()` creates a sibling instance without re-running a smart constructor, so validate in `init` (or keep the constructor private) - otherwise the invariant has a hole.
On the JVM the mapping rules are Java's: private setters and backing fields need the same JPA configuration, and the Kotlin all-open/no-arg plugins change proxies and lazy loading.
